articles.headline: Pensacola's $2.1M Hurricane Season Gamble
articles.dek: The city enters peak storm season with emergency reserves at their lowest point since 2018. Budget documents show why.
brief: Pensacola's emergency reserve fund sits at $2.1 million, down from $8.4 million in 2022
City documents show reserves were drawn down to cover infrastructure projects after federal reimbursements stalled
Peak hurricane season runs August through October, with NOAA predicting above-average Atlantic activity
articles.body:
The hurricane shutters stacked behind Pensacola's Public Works building tell one story. The city's balance sheet tells another.

As Pensacola enters the most dangerous stretch of the 2026 hurricane season, its emergency reserve fund holds $2.1 million — enough to cover roughly 72 hours of post-storm operations, according to budget documents obtained through a public records request. That's down from $8.4 million four years ago and represents the lowest reserve level since Hurricane Michael scraped the western Panhandle in 2018.

The math is uncomfortable. A direct hit from a Category 2 storm would likely require $15 million to $20 million in immediate response costs, based on the city's own post-storm assessments from hurricanes Sally in 2020 and Ida in 2021. Federal reimbursement through FEMA typically takes 18 to 24 months.

"We'd be operating on credit," said one city budget analyst who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss the matter publicly. "The money would come eventually. The question is what happens in between."

Where the money went

The reserve drawdown didn't happen in a single budget year. It accumulated across three fiscal cycles as the city faced a problem familiar to Gulf Coast municipalities: federal money promised but not yet delivered.

Budget documents show the city advanced $3.2 million from reserves in FY2024 to complete drainage improvements on 12th Avenue after FEMA reimbursement for Hurricane Sally damage stalled in a documentation dispute. Another $1.8 million went toward temporary repairs at the Port of Pensacola in early 2025, again while awaiting federal funds.

The reimbursements are still pending. FEMA Region 4 officials did not respond to requests for comment on the status of Pensacola's outstanding claims.

City Finance Director Maria Santos defended the approach during a budget workshop in June. "We don't have the luxury of waiting two years for Washington to process paperwork while our infrastructure fails," she said. "These were calculated decisions."

Calculated, perhaps. But the calculation assumed the reimbursements would arrive before the next storm did.

The insurance question

Pensacola carries $50 million in property coverage through the Florida Municipal Insurance Trust, with a $1 million deductible per occurrence. But property insurance covers buildings and equipment, not the immediate costs of emergency response — overtime for first responders, debris removal contracts, emergency shelter operations, fuel.

Those expenses fall on general fund reserves until FEMA's Public Assistance program kicks in. And FEMA only reimburses 75% of eligible costs. The city covers the rest.

The city's five-year capital plan, approved in March, projected reserves would rebuild to $5 million by September 2027 — assuming no major storm events and assuming federal reimbursements clear by year's end. Neither assumption is guaranteed.

NOAA's seasonal outlook, issued in May, predicted 17 to 24 named storms in the Atlantic basin this year, with 8 to 13 reaching hurricane strength. The agency called it a "well above average" season driven by warm sea surface temperatures and weakening La Niña conditions.

What happens if

City emergency management coordinator James Whitfield outlined the protocols during a council briefing in July. In a major storm event, Pensacola would activate mutual aid agreements with Escambia County and neighboring municipalities, access state emergency funds through the Division of Emergency Management, and begin the FEMA application process within 48 hours of a presidential disaster declaration.

"The systems work," Whitfield said. "They're designed for exactly this scenario."

What he didn't say: the systems work slowly. Mutual aid agreements provide personnel, not cash. State emergency funds are loans, not grants. And FEMA's process begins with damage assessments that can take weeks.

In the interim, the city would need to cover payroll, contracts, and emergency purchases from whatever cash reserves remain — plus whatever lines of credit it could secure.

Pensacola maintains a $10 million revolving line of credit with Hancock Whitney Bank for exactly this purpose. But credit isn't free money. Interest accrues. And borrowing against future revenues to cover current emergencies is a pattern that compounds over time.

The politics of preparedness

Emergency reserves rarely feature in campaign speeches. Voters notice potholes and parks, not balance sheets. That political reality shapes budget priorities in predictable ways.

The Pensacola City Council approved $4.6 million in FY2026 for streetscape improvements in the downtown core and $2.2 million for expanded recreational facilities at Bayview Park. Both projects polled well in community surveys. Both broke ground this spring.

No council member proposed redirecting those funds to emergency reserves. No constituent called to demand it.

"There's no constituency for saving money," said Howard Bates, a retired city planner who served under three Pensacola mayors. "People want services. They assume the emergency money will be there when they need it."

That assumption gets tested only when the storm hits.

The last major test came in September 2020, when Hurricane Sally made landfall near Gulf Shores, Alabama, and dumped 20 inches of rain on Pensacola in 12 hours. Flooding swamped downtown businesses, collapsed a section of the Three Mile Bridge, and left 130,000 customers without power for up to two weeks.

The city's direct costs exceeded $12 million. Reserves at the time held $6.8 million. The gap was covered through emergency appropriations, deferred maintenance, and eventually FEMA reimbursement — the same reimbursement still trickling in six years later.

September and forward

The city's fiscal year ends September 30. The FY2027 budget, scheduled for council approval in late September, projects reserve contributions of $800,000 — contingent on revenues meeting projections and no unplanned expenditures arising.

Peak hurricane season runs through October.

The gap between fiscal planning and meteorological reality is not unique to Pensacola. Municipalities across the Gulf Coast face the same calculus every year: spend on visible improvements that win elections or save for invisible disasters that may not come.

Pensacola has chosen spending. The next storm, whenever it arrives, will reveal whether that was prudent optimism or a $2.1 million gamble.

The hurricane shutters will come down from the Public Works building eventually. The budget math will take longer to resolve.

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Who's Buying Pensacola Beach? A Look at the Ownership Shift
articles.dek: Corporate LLCs now control 340 leasehold properties on the island, up from 89 five years ago. What that means for the beach's future.
brief: Corporate LLC ownership of Pensacola Beach leaseholds has increased 282% since 2021, according to Escambia County property records.
The Santa Rosa Island Authority reports rising concerns about absentee ownership and short-term rental saturation in residential zones.
Long-term residents say the shift has fundamentally changed the character of neighborhoods like Portofinno and Via de Luna.
articles.body:
The house at 1847 Via de Luna Drive sold three times in four years. First to a retired couple from Mobile. Then to an LLC registered in Wilmington, Delaware. Then to another LLC, this one traced to a holding company in Austin.

No one has lived there full-time since 2023. The lawn service comes Tuesdays. A cleaning crew rotates through on Saturdays. The rest of the week, the house cycles through vacation renters who park too many cars in the driveway and leave the garage lights on all night.

"We used to know everyone on this street," said Patricia Hendricks, who has held a leasehold four doors down since 1994. "Now I don't know anyone. They're not neighbors. They're guests."

What's happening on Via de Luna is happening across Pensacola Beach. A Flightline analysis of Escambia County property records and Santa Rosa Island Authority leasehold data shows that corporate LLCs now control 340 leasehold properties on the island, up from 89 in 2021. That's a 282% increase in five years.

The shift represents the most significant change in the island's ownership structure since the leasehold system was established in 1947.

The Numbers

Pensacola Beach operates under a unique arrangement. The federal government transferred Santa Rosa Island to Escambia County after World War II with the stipulation that it remain public land. Property owners don't own their lots outright. They hold 99-year leases administered by the Santa Rosa Island Authority.

There are roughly 2,100 leaseholds on the island. According to SRIA records, 340 are now held by LLCs, corporations or trusts with no identifiable local owner. Five years ago, that number was 89.

The acceleration began in 2022. That year, 47 leaseholds transferred to corporate entities. In 2023, the number jumped to 61. Last year, it hit 78.

"We've watched this trend build for several years," said SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio. "The board has discussed it multiple times. The question is what, if anything, we can or should do about it."

The authority has limited tools. Florida law restricts local governments from discriminating against corporate property owners. The leasehold agreements contain no provisions barring LLC ownership or requiring owner occupancy.

Where the Money Comes From

Tracing LLC ownership is difficult by design. Delaware, Wyoming and Nevada allow corporations to form without disclosing beneficial owners. Many of the LLCs holding Pensacola Beach leaseholds are registered in those states.

But patterns emerge in the data. At least 23 leaseholds are controlled by entities linked to Birmingham-based Beachside Holdings Group, a vacation rental investment firm. Another 14 trace to a network of LLCs associated with a Dallas real estate syndication company.

Representatives for neither company responded to interview requests.

Local real estate agents say institutional buyers began targeting Pensacola Beach around 2021, when pandemic-era demand for vacation rentals spiked and the island's relative affordability compared to Destin or Panama City Beach attracted attention.

"The word got out," said Mark Childress, a broker with Levin Rinke Realty who has handled beach transactions for 18 years. "National investors looked at our cap rates, looked at our occupancy numbers, and said this is where we want to be."

Median leasehold sale prices on Pensacola Beach have risen from $485,000 in 2020 to $847,000 this year, according to Emerald Coast Association of Realtors data.

The Rental Question

Not every LLC-owned property operates as a short-term rental. Some are second homes held in trusts for estate planning. Others are long-term rentals.

But the correlation is strong. SRIA records show 289 of the 340 corporate-owned leaseholds have active vacation rental registrations. That's 85%.

The proliferation of short-term rentals has strained infrastructure and changed the rhythm of residential streets. Hendricks, the Via de Luna resident, said she's called the Escambia County Sheriff's Office four times this year for noise complaints. She never called once in her first 25 years on the island.

"I understand people want to make money," she said. "But this isn't a resort. This is where people live. Or it used to be."

The SRIA conducted a community survey last year that found 67% of full-time residents believe short-term rentals have negatively affected their quality of life. The same survey found 71% support some form of rental density restrictions.

But implementation remains elusive. A proposed ordinance limiting rentals in certain zones died in committee last fall after property rights advocates argued it would devalue existing investments.

What's at Stake

The ownership shift carries implications beyond neighborhood character. Full-time residents provide the volunteer base for the island's fire department. They serve on the SRIA board. They patronize year-round businesses.

The Sandshaker Lounge, an island institution since 1973, closed in February. Owner Mike Swanson blamed the loss of local regulars. "Used to be I'd see the same faces every week," he told The Flightline at the time. "Now it's a new crowd every weekend. They don't know us. We don't know them."

Several other year-round businesses have reported similar struggles. The island's only hardware store reduced its hours last year. A dry cleaner shuttered.

Meanwhile, souvenir shops and beach rental outfitters have multiplied.

"The economy is shifting to serve visitors, not residents," said Dr. Angela Morrison, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies coastal development. "That's not inherently bad. But it's a choice with consequences."

The Path Forward

The SRIA board has scheduled a workshop for September to discuss potential responses. Options under consideration include requiring local property management for rental units, increasing lease fees for non-owner-occupied properties and advocating for state legislation allowing ownership restrictions.

None would reverse the trend. The 340 corporate-owned leaseholds aren't going anywhere. But proponents argue that slowing the pace of conversion could preserve what remains of the island's residential character.

Ghio, the SRIA director, said he's not optimistic about major changes. "There are a lot of competing interests," he said. "Property owners have rights. Investors have capital. We're trying to find balance in a system that wasn't designed for this."

Back on Via de Luna, Hendricks has started attending SRIA meetings. She's never been politically active. She's 73 years old and says she doesn't have the energy for a fight.

But she also doesn't want to leave.

"I built a life here," she said. "My husband's ashes are in the Gulf. This is home."

She paused and looked down the street toward the house that's sold three times.

"Or it was."
